# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

whys.g1: Borrowing a pair to test it first and keeping up with lots of voices at once are two different things I'd think about separately, both names are plain, and Diego's 'it costs too much for burgers' fits neither group, so leaving it alone is right.
whys.g2: Tomás's answer is about how he sits now rather than what would make it worth more, so it's off-topic, and it was kept out of the groups.

founder.order_why: Mostly logical, but 'who has to agree before they can buy' (14) comes after cost and price (12-13), separated from 'who decides' (10-11), so the buyer question gets split by the money questions.

screens.why2: The question asks two things, the step and its cost, in a 9-word box, and the hint's examples (*pay for a pilot*, *let us run a trial*) are business-sale words, not how I'd talk about someone buying glasses for themselves.
screens.why3: I know exactly what I want a hard-of-hearing person to do first: order a pair on our 15-day risk-free returns.
screens.why4: The only option is the founder-side escape *Leave this out of the study*, which fits the card's *I'm not sure* rule, and the box takes my step as typed.
screens.why5: The belief *Most deaf or hard-of-hearing adults would order a pair with free returns* keeps my words exactly, with *free returns* and *a pair* intact and no added *now*, timing or number.
screens.why7: The step is the right shape (base form, under 9 words, keeps *free returns*), but ordering a pair costs $599 and the screen neither asks for nor shows the free smaller step the card requires when a step costs money, so the soft yes would have nothing to name.
screens.instead: What's the first real step you'd want them to take? e.g. "order a pair with free returns" -- and since that costs money, what free step would come before it? e.g. "a look at the captions in a demo"

screens.why1: Right after I typed my first real step, it makes sense to see it back as strangers will hear it before Keel tests it.
screens.why2: "Order a pair with free returns" is exactly how I say it and how my customers say it; nothing to re-read.
screens.why3: Whether a deaf or hard-of-hearing adult would order a pair of glasses for themselves is a decision they make themselves, so they can answer it from their own life.
screens.why4: The step is kept whole at six words, with 'a pair' and 'free returns' intact, and it names what is ordered.
screens.why5: It is my step word for word, and the belief adds no 'now', no timing and no number I didn't write.
screens.why7: Ordering a pair costs the wearer $599 up front, even with free returns, so the card wants a free smaller step beside it; none is shown, which leaves the soft yes as a bare 'Probably yes' instead of 'Probably, after … first'.
screens.instead: Step: order a pair with free returns; smaller step (free): a free demo of the captions first, so the soft yes reads 'Probably, after a free demo of the captions first'.

screens.why1: Right after I set my first real step, and just before strangers see the study, it is the obvious moment to decide whether to collect the people who would actually try it.
screens.why2: "Offer a pilot?" with "Yes, ask them" or "No pilot" reads plainly on the first pass, and the hint says exactly what respondents will see and where I'll find the yeses.
screens.why3: Whether I want emails from deaf and hard-of-hearing people who'd try AirCaps is my own call about my own launch.
screens.why4: A yes/no choice is complete and distinct for this decision, and no escape option is needed.
screens.why5: My step was "order a pair with free returns", but the closing line respondents get is a generic "Would you try this for real?", so the free-returns order I typed does not reach them.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes get a line at the end: "Would you order a pair with 15-day free returns? Leave your email." (Yes, ask them / No pilot)

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions belongs in the last step before the link goes out, after the study itself is settled.
screens.why2: Plain words; 'credits' is Keel's own unit and the cost is stated outright, so I can answer on first read.
screens.why3: I can pick, but the screen asks me to judge by how she sounds, while what my deaf and hard-of-hearing respondents will judge is the written text and whether they can lipread her face, which the screen doesn't let me preview.
screens.why4: Two distinct, sensible choices, but both are framed only as a voice ('Hear Daphne'); for my audience the missing preview is the face and the captions, and there is no text-only option for people who won't use the video at all.
screens.why5: It names my respondents as I typed them and leaks nothing of AirCaps or the roles to them.
screens.instead: Who should ask deaf and hard-of-hearing adults your questions? Every question is captioned on screen and people can type or tap; preview each interviewer's face and captions (and voice): Daphne ▶ Watch · 5 s / Saskia ▶ Watch · 5 s / Text only, no video.

screens.why1: Choosing how strangers answer belongs here, right after picking who asks and just before sending, so it is obvious why it is asked.
screens.why2: Each option says in plain words what the respondent will do (watch Daphne, read and tap, or pick), so I can answer on first reading.
screens.why3: I know my people: many deaf and hard-of-hearing adults would rather read than follow a voice on video, so I can answer from what I know of them.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and complete, and the Daphne one says every question is also written on screen, which keeps it workable for a deaf audience; typing as well as speaking covers non-speaking people like Andrea.
screens.why5: It names my respondents as I typed them (deaf or hard-of-hearing adults) and keeps my pick, Read and tap, with nothing of AirCaps leaking into the respondent-facing choice.

screens.why1: After choosing how people answer, choosing who gets a link is the obvious last step before sending.
screens.why2: The three choices read plainly to me on first read, though 'Contacts page' assumes I know Keel's own layout.
screens.why3: I know whether I am reaching deaf and hard-of-hearing people I know by name (our waitlist and testers) or posting in a community group.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover the cases, but the Google sign-in on the open link is a real barrier for some deaf community spaces and is stated as a fixed condition rather than an option, and there is no mix of named people and a group.
screens.why5: Nothing of my product or roles is changed; it is a sending choice and my pick 'People I know by name' is kept.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? -- People I know by name (each gets their own link) / A list I found with Keel (one link each, I send them) / A group or forum I post one open link to (each person signs in, then is interviewed) / Some of each

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits beside a number, but the headline names Existing sacrifice at 1 of 7 when Price at 0 of 7 on both legs looks like the worse card, so I can't see why that one decides it under 'the worst of all its cards'.
screens.why_b2: Each card reads plainly: what is counted (lose 12+ conversations, valued at $599+, decided alone, said yes), over 7 people, against a bar of 5 of 7.
screens.why_b3: Buyer and payer and Commitment are my lines word for word and Price is recognisable, but Existing sacrifice is stated as 'about 12 conversations a month' when my estimate was $200 to $1,500 a year, and the cards jump from 4 to 6 with no 5.
screens.why_b4: The status lines ('they lose less today than you estimated', 'they value it below your price') say which way it went, but nothing tells me what to change, such as re-pricing, leading with the free-caption plan or testing a lower price for the glasses.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is shown on every card but never called a small sample, and 'Commitment: Holding up, 6 of 7 said yes' sits unremarked beside 0 of 7 valuing it at my price, which reads as more buying intent than free returns can carry.
screens.instead: Not holding up on money: none of 7 value AirCaps at $599 or $20 a month, and only 1 of 7 loses a dozen conversations a month, so 6 of 7 ordering under free returns is a trial, not a sale. Re-test with a lower glasses price, a free-captions-only offer and a bigger sample.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits right beside its deciding count, 1 of 7 at 12 or more against a bar of 5 of 7, and the 'smaller than you think' line says which way it missed.
screens.why_b2: The strip's own line shows one cell per person, 7 counted, bar at 5 of 7, but the 0-5-10-15 conversation axis and the 'about 12' marker sit over a strip whose marker is at 5 people, and the unit label 'conversations of the conversations they are in a month' is garbled, so I had to look twice to see which 5 and 12 were which.
screens.why_b3: I put Existing sacrifice in money, $200 to $1,500 a year that people already spend on captioning apps and hearing-aid extras, and this card tests a count of conversations lost per month in a half-sentence that is not a belief I typed or would recognise as mine.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates the count and points to the Price card; it doesn't say what 4 to 8 lost conversations a month means for my price or wedge.
screens.why_b5: The count line names all 7 and says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and every person's number and reading is listed, so nothing claims more than the 7 answers carry.
screens.instead: Test my belief as I typed it, 'Deaf and hard-of-hearing adults already spend $200 to $1,500 a year on captioning apps and hearing-aid extras', ask what they spent last year in dollars, and say what a miss means for the $599 price.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits right beside its deciding numbers, 0 of 7 at $599 up front and 0 of 7 at $20 a month against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know the result and why at once.
screens.why_b2: Each ladder shows its counts per band, my $599 and $20 marked as a band's low edge, and the strip of 7 against with the marker at 5, so what is counted, over whom and where the bar sits are plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: I recognise $599 up front and $20 a month, but my Pro plan is optional (the free plan has unlimited captions), and the belief and the rule line treat the $20 as owed by everyone, which drops a term I attached.
screens.why_b4: The So line tells me where they cluster ($250 to under $599, 6 of 7) but then only points to the Insights tab; it never says what that means for my price, like testing an up-front price under $599 or leading with a borrow or demo pair, which is what the quotes keep asking for.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', and nothing claims more than the seven who answered; 'fewer than 2 in 3' undersells a 0 of 7 rather than overstating it.
screens.instead: None of 7 would pay $599 up front; 6 of 7 put it at $250 to under $599, and the $20 Pro plan is optional on top. Before trusting $599, try a lower up-front price or a borrow-first pair, which four of them asked for.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not reached' sits right beside '0 of 7 named your price or more · nothing to ask', so I see at once that this decides nothing because nobody got to my $599 price.
screens.why_b2: The bars are all 0 and the strip draws 5 ghost cells while 7 people are listed, so I need a second look at the count line ('not asked: 7 named less') to see that the chart counts nobody and that the 5 is the floor, not the people.
screens.why_b3: 'Ability to pay' and my $599 up front plus $20 a month are recognisable, but the line 'could find it in money they already spend on this' is Keel's derived belief, not one I typed or checked, and the card calls it mine.
screens.why_b4: 'Ability to pay waits until at least 5 do' tells me it is on hold, but it does not say the plain next step, which is that my Price is the blocker and I have to fix it before this card can say anything.
screens.why_b5: It claims nothing beyond the 7 people, keeps n visible, and says outright that the card is not reached and decides nothing.
screens.instead: Not reached: none of the 7 would pay $599, so nobody was asked where the money would come from. Fix the Price first; this card can only speak once at least 5 people name $599 or more.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside the number that decides it, 6 of 7 decided alone against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and why.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the seven people's last purchase by who had to agree, shows 6 for and 1 against, and puts my bar at 5 of 7 on the strip, so all three are plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: The title 'Buyer and payer' and the belief 'The deaf or hard-of-hearing adult decides, and nobody else must agree first' are word for word what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates the count (they decide alone, 1 of 7 needed agreement); it never tells me that who decides is not my problem and the price is, nor what Walter's case, where a spouse had to agree, means for how I sell.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible as 7 answered and 7 counted, the small group is called 'a lean, not a call', and nothing claims more than the six who decided alone.
screens.instead: Holding up, a lean on 7: 6 decided alone, so who signs off isn't what's blocking you; the price is. Walter needed his spouse's agreement, so make the free returns and HSA/FSA easy to show a partner.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 6 of 7 said yes and bar 5 of 7, so I know it held and which number decided it.
screens.why_b2: The counts over 7 and the marker at 5 are plain, but the chart's second option says Probably yes while the rule line says probably, after a free try-on of a working pair first, so I had to look twice to see what that soft yes actually offered.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Commitment and its belief is word for word the one I checked: most deaf or hard-of-hearing adults would order a pair with free returns.
screens.why_b4: Book them into it is vague: into what, ordering $599 glasses? It also says nothing about the Price card, where 0 of 7 valued it at $599, so I don't learn what this yes means for the idea.
screens.why_b5: The count line honestly calls 7 people a lean, not a call, but the So line acts on 6 of 7 as if it were firm, when a yes made easy by free returns sits against 0 of 7 at my price.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 say they'd order a pair with free returns, a lean from 7 people; but none valued it at $599, so treat this as a willingness to try, and offer the free try-on to see who keeps the pair after 15 days.

screens.why_b1: The box opens on Not holding up with 0 of 7 at $599 or more up front and 0 of 7 at $20 or more a month against a bar of 5 of 7, so the verdict and the number that decides it sit together.
screens.why_b3: The Price name and the belief line, $599 up front then $20 a month, are the price ladder I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: Under the generic 'When a line fails' heading the screen gives me groups but never says what to do, such as making the 15-day returns read as a trial, proving the glasses on group cross-talk, or testing a price nearer $250 to $599 with under $10 a month.
screens.why_b5: The n stays visible (7 against, 6 asked here, Amaka never saw it), each group carries its count of 2, and nothing is claimed beyond those six people.
screens.why_b6: I did not know that people want to borrow a pair before ordering even with free returns, that picking up many voices (audience questions, eleven at a family lunch) is what would make it worth more, or that most put it at $250 to under $599 with under $10 a month while a one-sided user manages by taking the end seat.
screens.instead: Say plainly what it means: they want to try before buying even with 15-day returns, so sell the returns as a trial; show it keeping up with many voices at once; and most valued it at $250 to under $599 with under $10 a month, so test that price next.

screens.why1: As the first screen it's an obvious check that I belong in a study about talking with hearing people, and nothing before it has asked it.
screens.why2: "Hearing people" is how we say it in my world, and the whole question is plain on first read or hearing.
screens.why3: I know without guessing whether I've been chatting with hearing folks at work, the shops or with family this week.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it completely for a gate, and the gate rightly carries no escape.
screens.why5: It is the founder's own segment words almost exactly, and nothing about a product, app or caption device leaks to me.
screens.why6: Short, one question, and yes-or-no is easy to answer on one hearing, though the spoken form never actually says "Yes or no" at the end.
screens.instead: Do you talk face to face with hearing people every week? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after I said I talk with hearing people every week, showing me the idea before asking about it is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Live captions, glasses and eye contact are things I deal with all the time, so I take it in on one read, though saying 'lightweight glasses' twice and 'the app' is a bit clunky.
screens.why3: Keeping eye contact while trying to catch what hearing people say face to face is exactly my everyday struggle.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: It names the product on purpose as an idea card and talks about conversations and eye contact in plain words, with no insider terms for people like me leaking in.
screens.why6: Four short sentences that say well aloud, with no symbols or parentheses, only a slightly repetitive second line.
screens.instead: Imagine AirCaps, an app on lightweight glasses that shows live captions of nearby speech. When people near you talk, their words appear as captions inside the lens. The people building it believe it would let you read the words while keeping eye contact.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, asking how often I already miss out in conversations is an obvious place to start on what I do today.
screens.why2: "Go without the thread" isn't how I'd say it; I'd say I couldn't follow or lost track, so I had to read it twice to be sure what it meant.
screens.why3: It happens to me all the time, but counting a whole month of conversations means I'd be guessing; a week I could actually count.
screens.why4: A box for the number, None, and I can't recall covers every true answer without overlap.
screens.why5: Nothing about the product or anyone's labels for people like me shows up; it just asks about my conversations.
screens.why6: It's short and the escape is said last, but "go without the thread" heard once is the kind of phrase I'd have to ask to have repeated.
screens.why7: The box stays on one count of conversations per month and both sides stay open with the one escape, but the verb is the vague kind the card warns against instead of the plain thing I see go: following the talk.
screens.instead: Last month, about how many conversations with hearing people were too fast or too noisy for you to follow? [ box ] conversations last month · None · I can't recall

screens.why1: A price question after the idea card makes sense, but it comes right after one question about missed conversations, and the kicker calls it 'What you do today' when it asks me to price glasses I've never used, so it feels abrupt.
screens.why2: 'Worth to you up front' and 'a month' are how I'd talk about paying for glasses and then a captioning subscription, and the dollar bands are plain.
screens.why3: I know what I've paid for hearing aids and caption apps, so I have a feel for it, but for glasses I've only just heard of I'd be partly guessing.
screens.why4: Both ladders run in order with no amount in two rungs and include 'I wouldn't pay for this', and 'I can't say' sits apart as the escape.
screens.why5: The only product I see is the idea card shown on purpose, the price asks are in my words, and nothing of the founder's own terms for people like me leaks in.
screens.why6: Each step is one short question with four options I can hold, then two, and the single 'Or say: I can't say' comes last; '$599 to under $1,000' is the longest phrase but it says fine.
screens.why7: This is the price-then-plan shape: two six-rung ladders on one measure each (an up-front sum, then a monthly fee), each with a band edge at what is presumably the founder's low ($599, $20), two bands below plus 'I wouldn't pay' against and three bands for, and the one escape apart.
screens.instead: Kicker 'An idea to consider' rather than 'What you do today'; otherwise the same: What would AirCaps be worth to you up front? Under $250 · $250 to under $599 · $599 to under $1,000 · $1,000 to under $2,500 · $2,500 or more · I wouldn't pay for this · I can't say.

screens.why1: Right after I gave a price, asking what would make it worth more is an obvious follow-up.
screens.why2: It says my answer back as I would put it, about $250 to $600 up front, and the question is short and plain.
screens.why3: I can say what I'd want from captions in a noisy room, but I only know AirCaps from the card, so part of it is a guess.
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options.
screens.why5: AirCaps was named on the idea card on purpose, and nothing else of the founder's plan or terms reaches me.
screens.why6: Two short sentences, one question, said easily once.

screens.why1: Right after I gave a price for AirCaps, it makes sense to ask whether I could just buy it myself or whether my spouse, my insurer or a rehab counselor would have a say. People like me run into that with hearing aids all the time.
screens.why2: It is short and plain, and after the idea card I know "something like this" means a captioning or hearing device.
screens.why3: I have never bought captioning glasses, so I would answer from my last hearing-aid or captioning-app purchase, and that is partly a guess about whether it counts as "like this."
screens.why4: The four run cleanly from my own choice to someone else's, and "It was someone else's call" covers the insurer or vocational rehab paying. "I can't say" fits as the way out.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's pitch or terms leaks in, and "anyone else" is how I would say it.
screens.why6: It is one short question with four short options I can hold, and the escape is said last. The spoken "You decided on your own" only swaps the pronoun from the screen's "I."
screens.why7: Nobody else is tested, and the card's four past-tense answers are all here in order with "Someone else" in the second slot. One answer supports the belief and three refute it, and "I can't say" is present and set apart.
screens.instead: The last time you paid for a hearing aid or captioning tool, did anyone else have to agree? I decided on my own · Someone else had to agree · Several people had to agree · It was someone else's call · I can't say

screens.why1: After the price and who has to agree, asking whether I'd actually order a pair is the obvious last question, though the 'What you do today' kicker is odd over a what-if.
screens.why2: Ordering a pair of glasses with free returns is how I'd say it myself, and I get it on one read or one hearing.
screens.why3: I decide what I buy for my own hearing, so I can answer this from how I'd really act.
screens.why4: Four distinct answers from a firm yes to a firm no, and my true answer, a hesitant yes, is there as Probably yes.
screens.why5: The step keeps the founder's 'free returns' and 'a pair', and the name AirCaps comes from the idea card shown on purpose, so nothing leaks.
screens.why6: Short, one question, four short options read as a list I can hold, and no escape to add a second list.
screens.why7: The first option is the founder's own step in its own verb, the soft yes is a yes to the same step, the order is two for and two against, and there is no escape, as the card requires.
